book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Three doors into the same search
episodes.subtitle: Lexical search beyond strict Boolean

scenes.title: A missing word. A mysterious result.
scenes.claim: A missing typed word does not prove semantic retrieval
scenes.narration: You search for apple, orange, and banana. A result contains apple and orange, but no banana. Has the search engine understood your meaning? Perhaps. But ordinary word matching can produce exactly this result. Welcome to the surprisingly flexible world of lexical search.

scenes.title: Keep the little universe fixed
scenes.claim: The same records and analysed terms support different rules
scenes.narration: Meet four records. A contains all three query terms. B contains apple and orange. C contains only apple. D contains pear and grape. These cards show which terms occur, not their frequencies or document lengths. We will change the admission rule while keeping the records fixed.

scenes.title: Door one: bring every term
scenes.claim: All three required → A
scenes.narration: At the first door, every term is compulsory. Apple AND orange AND banana admits only A. B and C are excluded before scoring, along with D. A ranker can order the survivors, but cannot recover a record that never entered its candidate set.

scenes.title: Door two: two will do
scenes.claim: Minimum match: two of three → A and B
scenes.narration: At the second door, the system requires at least two of the three terms. A and B enter. C and D stay outside. This minimum-match rule is still entirely lexical. Its evidence comes from analysed query terms matching indexed document terms.

scenes.title: Door three: any one is enough
scenes.claim: Any-match eligibility → A, B and C
scenes.narration: At the third door, any one matching term is sufficient. A, B, and C may compete. D still cannot. This eligibility rule is the union of the posting lists, expressible as Boolean OR. A separate scoring function, such as BM twenty-five, adds graded lexical evidence.

scenes.title: Getting in is not winning
scenes.claim: Illustrative order B, A, C is stipulated, not calculated
scenes.narration: Now keep that any-match rule fixed. Suppose the scoring rule orders the candidates B, A, C. This order is stipulated, not calculated from our cards. More distinct matches do not guarantee a higher BM twenty-five score: rarity, repetition, and document length also affect the contributions.

scenes.title: The list has an edge
scenes.claim: Top-2 keeps B and A; C qualified, D never did
scenes.narration: A top-two output keeps B and A. C was eligible but fell below the output boundary. D never qualified. A reported match count, an ordered list, and a viewable set describe different properties. A display limit does not reveal the scoring method or prove a global top-k computation.

scenes.title: Three controls. One lexical engine.
scenes.claim: Admission · ranking · output boundary
scenes.narration: Separate three controls: who may compete, how candidates are ordered, and how many leaders are retained. All three doors can use the same terms and inverted index. Non-Boolean behaviour does not establish non-lexical retrieval. Next, watch one weak query term cause two very different kinds of trouble.

episodes.title: One bad word, two kinds of damage
episodes.subtitle: Exclusion under AND, distortion under BM25

scenes.title: The troublemaker joins the query
scenes.claim: Here, foolish is a weak substitute for delulu
scenes.narration: Suppose you search for delulu, job, interview, and expectations. You add foolish as a weak attempt at a synonym. The engine does not know why you chose it. The same extra term can shut useful records out, or give distracting records extra scoring evidence.

scenes.title: Two records from the Evidence Lab
scenes.claim: A matches the original four terms; F adds foolish
scenes.narration: Record A is Delulu expectations during a job interview. It contains the four original terms, but no foolish. Record F is Why foolish job applicants misread the interview. It contains foolish, job, and interview, but lacks delulu and expectations.

scenes.title: AND turns a word into a lock
scenes.claim: With all five terms required, both A and F are excluded
scenes.narration: Under implied AND, foolish becomes compulsory. A met the original four conditions, but the added condition now excludes it. F is also excluded because other required terms are missing. The extra word changes admission. No downstream ranker can rescue A from this closed gate.

scenes.title: Any-match lets the records compete
scenes.claim: A stays eligible; F gains another matching contribution
scenes.narration: Under any-match BM twenty-five, A remains eligible. Its existing matches still provide evidence. F is eligible too, and gains another contribution from foolish. The bad term has changed jobs: it no longer vetoes A, but can affect the competition.

scenes.title: Rarity is not a synonym detector
scenes.claim: In the lab collection, only F contains foolish
scenes.narration: In the lab collection, only F contains foolish. Inverse document frequency gives that rare matching term extra weight. Rarity does not make foolish a good synonym, or F a better answer. A weak term can pull the ranking toward the wrong evidence. We assert no numerical ranking here.

scenes.title: A flatter curve cannot fix meaning
scenes.claim: Saturation limits repetition, not a term's conceptual weakness
scenes.narration: Term-frequency saturation cannot identify a poor query term. It limits the benefit of repeating the same term within a document. It does not understand that foolish was a questionable choice in the first place. Less binary word evidence is still word evidence.

scenes.title: Change the representation of the need
scenes.claim: Test the query term as well as the retrieval rule
scenes.narration: Neither mechanism malfunctioned. Each followed its rules using the query it received. The practical move is to inspect the term: does it express your need, and what happens when you remove it? Changing a required term alters admission; changing an optional term can alter scores and the candidate set.

scenes.title: The gate and the magnet
scenes.claim: A flawed query can cause exclusion or distort scoring
scenes.narration: Remember the two consequences. Under all-term AND, the weak word acts like a gate that can exclude useful records. Under any-match ranking, it can act like a magnet pulling scores toward distracting matches. Good retrieval over a poor representation can still produce a poor search. Next: where did your missing word go?

episodes.title: The four lives of a missing word
episodes.subtitle: Query processing and the limits of a result screen

scenes.title: One screen. Four possible histories.
scenes.claim: These are possible mechanisms, not product diagnoses
scenes.narration: A useful-looking result lacks a word you typed. A tiny mystery, with at least four possible histories. The word may have disappeared, changed, become optional, or matched somewhere you cannot see. Several of these mechanisms can operate together in one search.

scenes.title: History one: removed during analysis
scenes.claim: Routine string preparation can remove a typed term
scenes.narration: First, routine analysis may remove it. You type the job interview. An illustrative stop-word rule discards the, so retrieval receives job interview. Tokenisation, case folding, stemming, and stop-word handling prepare strings for matching. These operations do not themselves imply artificial intelligence or understanding of meaning.

scenes.title: History two: changed during rewriting
scenes.claim: Transformation changes what retrieval receives
scenes.narration: Second, an upstream rewrite may change it. You type delulu job expectations. A mapping replaces delulu with unrealistic. Retrieval receives different words. Query transformation can correct, map, expand, restructure, or split a request. This is distinct from routine analysis, and the example is not a claim about a named product.

scenes.title: History three: retained, but optional
scenes.claim: Other matches can suffice, even if this term has no postings
scenes.narration: Third, the word may survive but be optional. An any-match rule admits a record containing job and interview without delulu. The optional term might even have no posting list anywhere in the index. Other matches can still compete. Under strict AND, a required unmatched term would instead empty the result set.

scenes.title: History four: matched out of view
scenes.claim: A snippet shows less than the indexed record
scenes.narration: Fourth, the term may match evidence outside the visible excerpt. A title says Job interview expectations, while the indexed abstract contains delulu. Other searchable fields, expanded terms, an older indexed version, or off-page evidence can also matter. Inspect what the system indexes before concluding that no lexical match occurred.

scenes.title: Four jobs between you and the index
scenes.claim: Analysis · execution rules · understanding · transformation
scenes.narration: Keep four jobs separate. Analysis prepares strings. Execution rules decide which clauses are required, optional, or subject to minimum match. Understanding interprets phrases, entities, dates, or intent. Transformation actually changes the retrieval input. Understanding can inform a decision without changing a single query word.

scenes.title: A modern front door, a lexical engine
scenes.claim: Query rewriting is a stage, not a retrieval method
scenes.narration: A system can accept a natural-language question, interpret it with a language model, and construct a Boolean query. Analysis and execution then feed ordinary lexical retrieval. Artificial intelligence at the front does not identify the engine behind it. Understanding and rewriting are pipeline stages, not proofs of dense retrieval.

scenes.title: Ask the pipeline, not just the screen
scenes.claim: Inspect processed queries, admission rules and indexed fields
scenes.narration: Ask what query reached retrieval, which clauses were compulsory, and which fields were searchable. A screenshot or product name cannot settle the architecture. To bridge a vocabulary gap, a system can change the query while keeping lexical matching, or change the representation used for retrieval. Part Two explores that second route.
